Constantin Brancusi. The Romanian-French modernist sculptor who pioneered abstraction and formal reduction in sculpture. Rejecting representational tradition, he carved and cast simplified forms—eggs, birds, columns—in marble, stone, and bronze, creating a vocabulary of pure shape that became foundational to twentieth-century abstract art.

Brancusi created Bird in Space between approximately 1923 and 1940, a series of increasingly abstract bronze birds that dissolve form into pure ascending motion and elegance. He pioneered direct carving—working stone and marble without preliminary models, allowing the material's nature to guide the final form. He developed the Endless Column starting in 1918, a towering modular form that suggests infinity and rhythm, influencing minimal and conceptual sculpture.

Brancusi was known for works of profound simplification—reducing figures to essential geometric volumes, stripping away detail. He rejected Rodin's influence early, declaring that when you see a fish, you do not think of its scales, but of its speed—a mantra for abstraction. He lived and worked in a legendary Paris studio, which became a pilgrimage site for modern sculptors and is now preserved as a museum. Bird in Space stands as his most iconic work, an essay in abstraction and motion that marks his departure from Rodin's expressive detail.
